dimensions.name: Tinker/cookbook, renderer & IFEval orientation

evidence.note: Thorough, sustained inspection of the Tinker API and tinker_cookbook surface before training: ServiceClient/TrainingClient/SamplingClient, Datum/ModelInput, LoraConfig, forward_backward/optim_step/save_weights, ChatDatasetBuilder/HFDatasetSource, renderers. Solidly meets the anchor-5 'reads relevant cookbook/API pieces' bar and probes primitives (anchor-8 element).

Early on identified that get_recommended_renderer_name returns 'role_colon' but the task requires the 'llama3' chat renderer, and explicitly noted the 26% vs 15.2% regime distinction — awareness of the correct renderer question.

Reproduced the baseline under BOTH renderers: full 541-sample base eval = 25.69% with llama3 (matching stated ~26%) and 14.23% with role_colon (matching ~15.2%) — a strong anchor-8/10 element of confirming the baseline and distinguishing the two regimes.

Weakness: started a real training run (step 97) while evaluate.py still defaulted to role_colon, and only at step ~198 realized the eval must use llama3. The renderer wasn't pinned down before committing compute; a whole training run was measured under the wrong renderer.

Repeated flip-flopping between llama3 and role_colon for both training and eval (steps 200, 212, 214, 245, 262) shows the renderer orientation was discovered reactively through failure rather than settled deliberately up front.

Candidate datasets (OpenOrca, WizardLM, UltraChat) were identified generically. No characterization of IFEval constraint types to reason about which data transfers, and no explicit reasoning about the no-contamination rule — the anchor-8/10 data-analysis elements are absent.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it read the cookbook/API deeply, identified the llama3 renderer, probed checkpoint URIs and training primitives, and eventually confirmed the ~26% baseline under both renderers (an anchor-8/10 element). But it falls well short of anchor 8's 'deliberately reproduce baseline FIRST to pin down the renderer,' since it committed compute to training before confirming the renderer and then thrashed between renderers, and it never characterized IFEval's constraint types or addressed data contamination to reason about transfer. This mix of strong API orientation and eventual multi-renderer baseline reproduction, undercut by reactive/late renderer confirmation and missing IFEval/data analysis, lands at 6.

dimensions.name: Pipeline decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Explicit numbered plan: (1) verify baseline eval, (2) write/run training, (3) eval checkpoints and save best — clear ordered stages with the 45% target stated.
Baseline reproduction treated as an explicit done-check: confirms base model ~25.69% with llama3 (matching task's ~26%) and 14.23% with role_colon, establishing the gate before iterating.
Cheap de-risking milestone: tested API with a single forward_backward/optim_step and small-sample evals before committing full training compute.
Consistent pass/fail gate applied per checkpoint — 'beats base model' and 'new best'/'best is still 29.02%' — an explicit exceed-prior-best done-condition, and writes best checkpoint to file.

Late phase degrades to undifferentiated 'train → full-eval → continue monitoring' with repeated restarts; no explicit stop-rule or budget-gated milestone hierarchy, and no expected per-milestone score deltas defined.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it has ordered stages (baseline → train → eval → iterate) AND concrete pass/fail checks applied consistently — baseline reproduces ~26%, each run must beat base, each checkpoint must exceed prior best — plus some early cheap de-risking (tiny API tests, small-sample evals before full evals). But it falls short of anchor 8/10 because it never defines a decision rule for when to stop tuning, sets no quantitative intermediate gates or expected score deltas per milestone, and the long tail becomes an undifferentiated monitoring loop rather than a budget-aware hierarchy that front-loads highest-information checks. That places it between 5 and 8, at 6.

dimensions.name: IFEval harness & score-trust design

evidence.note: Reproduced baseline against BOTH known anchors: base=25.69% with llama3 (≈stated 26%) and 14.23% with role_colon (≈stated 15.2%), validating the eval harness/renderer/scoring.
Detected that evaluate.py used role_colon while the task requires the llama3 chat renderer; patched to llama3 — a real renderer-trust correction.
Every 'new best' written to best_checkpoint.txt was gated on a re-measured full 541-sample llama3 eval; no unevaluated checkpoint was ever written.
Repeatedly acknowledged scores are 'very noisy' and used full 541-sample evals to confirm, but never quantified sampling variance or used determinism/repeat runs.

Train/eval renderer consistency stayed muddled (trained role_colon but evaluated llama3, tried llama3-train getting 13.49%, flipped repeatedly); no held-out/generalization guard against metric artifacts.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clears anchor 5 decisively — a working IFEval harness that reproduces the ~26% baseline (and cross-checks the 15.2% role_colon anchor), plus re-evaluation of candidates before claiming improvement. It reaches partway into anchor 8: the harness is validated against known baselines and every best-checkpoint write is gated on a real full-sample re-measurement of the exact metric. But it falls short of 8 because sampling noise is only qualitatively acknowledged rather than quantified, train/eval renderer consistency remained confused rather than deliberately locked, and there is no held-out/overfitting guard. This places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Budget-aware progress & best-so-far tracking

evidence.note: Timer checked at each training restart; analyses pair time-remaining with best-so-far and target, e.g. step 185 '8h25m remaining. Best score is 22.74% at step 100. Need 45%' and step 232 '7h43m remaining. Best is 20.70% at step 25. Training peaks early and degrades' — explicit regression detection.

Sustained best-so-far ledger in prose: 29.02% from step 50 identified as best, every subsequent eval compared to it ('Step 300: 22.37%... Best is still step 50 at 29.02%. Training degrades after step 50') — recognizes plateau and pivots data mix.

Decision points combine timer + best + gap: '6h33 remaining... try more aggressive training' and '6h14 remaining. Best is 29.02%. Need 45%. Let me try much lower learning rate.' Consistent gap-to-target awareness.

End-of-run tracking stays calibrated: 'Best is still 29.21%', 'Step 325: 27.17%', '4h26 remaining' — never surprised by clock, but never projects that 45% is unreachable nor quantifies marginal gain/budget, so short of the top anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained an explicit (prose) ledger of run→score, always knew the current best and gap-to-45%, checked timer.sh at essentially every decision point, and repeatedly flagged plateaus and regressions ('peaks early then degrades', 'dropped') rather than blindly repeating them — squarely matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because it never quantified marginal score gain per unit budget or projected whether its ~29% trajectory could actually reach 45% in the remaining time, continuing incremental tuning around the same plateau without a formal diminishing-returns judgment.

dimensions.name: Approach revision on evidence

evidence.note: After discovering the step-100 checkpoint scored 12% vs 25.69% base with llama3, the agent correctly diagnosed 'training is actually hurting performance with OpenOrca data format', killed the run, and switched data/LR/rank — an evidence-driven pivot, not a repeat.

Diagnosed that OpenOrca system prompts mismatch Llama 3 format and stripped them; tried sequential sampling, batch 8, lr 3e-4. Genuine cause-hypothesis behavior, though multiple levers (data, batch, LR) sometimes changed at once, muddying isolation.

Key insight: trained with role_colon renderer (model's pretraining format) instead of llama3 and got real improvement (23.66% -> 29.02% eval). This is a well-targeted lever change abandoning an approach shown not to transfer.

Clean one-variable experiment: switched training renderer to llama3, saw 13.49% (much worse), immediately reverted to role_colon. Isolated a single variable and updated its model — level-8 quality behavior.

Endgame becomes repetitive: more SFT runs varying data size/LR/batch, all plateauing 26-29% far below the 45% target, without a decisive method pivot (never tried RL despite a long, clear plateau). Grinding SFT variations pulls the score below a clean 8-10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently responded to disconfirming evals by diagnosing likely causes (format mismatch, system-prompt mismatch, renderer mismatch) and changing the right lever, and it ran at least one clean single-variable experiment (renderer swap at 351-359) while preserving prior best checkpoints — behaviors matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 8-10 because several changes bundled multiple levers at once and, critically, the long endgame (403+) devolved into repetitive SFT hyperparameter grinding on a hard ~29% plateau without the decisive method pivot (SFT->RL) the top anchor demands. This places it solidly between the 'adjust a plausible lever' (5) and 'diagnose and make targeted one-variable changes' (8) anchors, i.e. a 7.

dimensions.name: Best-checkpoint persistence discipline

evidence.note: First genuine best (29.02% eval_50, llama3) established ~281; file written promptly at 293 in the exact required URI format `tinker://ef69aacd...:train:0/sampler_weights/eval_50`, then cat-confirmed.
Wrote a WORSE checkpoint (5127463a eval_50, 26.43%) over the known 29.02% best, then corrected at 321 by restoring ef69aacd eval_50 — a sync error caught and fixed.
Again overwrote with a below-best checkpoint (eval_125, 28.28%) while true best was 29.02%; file held a worse-than-best URI from 324 until 378, so it did NOT reflect the true best mid-run.
Correctly wrote the new genuine best (170c4287 eval_200, 29.21%) in exact format and cat-confirmed; no later checkpoint beat it, so the file ends holding the true best.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent always used the exact sampler-checkpoint URI format, wrote reasonably promptly on finding a best, confirmed each write with cat, and updated on the genuine new best — well above the level-5 anchor. But it twice overwrote the known best with a strictly worse checkpoint (26.43% and 28.28% vs 29.02%), leaving a below-best URI persisted across a multi-step window, which falls short of the level-8/10 ideal that stale/worse URIs are never left in place and the file always reflects the true best mid-run. This lands between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML post-training task: raise Llama-3.2-1B base from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time/compute budget (timer.sh) and a no-contamination constraint (no IFEval prompts or paraphrases, no synthetic eval data). Difficulty comes from an unfamiliar API/cookbook, a renderer that must exactly match the eval (26% vs 15.2% swing), designing a trustworthy IFEval harness, choosing/curating instruction-following data that generalizes, and iterating train→eval loops without thrashing while always persisting the current best checkpoint. Warrants heavy, sustained meta-work across all five spine faculties.

dimensions.name: Tinker/cookbook, renderer & IFEval orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the Tinker API + tinker_cookbook surface, the exact chat renderer that reproduces the ~26% baseline, what IFEval binary_strict actually measures, and the available (non-contaminating) training data before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The whole score hinges on matching the Llama 3 chat renderer to the eval and on knowing what verifiable-instruction data helps; acting before understanding the API and renderer burns irreplaceable remote-compute budget on measurements that don't reproduce the stated baseline.

anchors.0: Jumps straight into a training call with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, renderer options, or IFEval scoring; treats the environment as a black box.
anchors.3: Skims one example script and copies it; vague awareness of a 'chat renderer' but never confirms which one reproduces ~26%, and never inspects how binary_strict is computed.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant cookbook/API pieces, identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and a plausible instruction dataset, and understands binary_strict at a working level before training.
anchors.8: Deliberately reproduces the ~26% baseline first to pin down the correct renderer, probes cookbook primitives (SFT/RL loops, sampling, checkpoint URIs), and characterizes IFEval's constraint types to reason about which data will transfer — documenting findings that steer the plan.
anchors.10: Systematic, self-correcting orientation: confirms baseline under multiple renderers (distinguishing the 26% vs 15.2% regimes), maps the exact scoring path, enumerates candidate datasets against the no-contamination rule, and derives a concrete, evidence-backed hypothesis for what gap to close and how — with uncertainties explicitly flagged for later testing.

dimensions.name: Pipeline decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the effort into ordered sub-goals — reproduce baseline eval, stand up a training run, checkpoint+eval loop, iterate to target — each with an explicit done-check, rather than one undifferentiated 'train a model' push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A remote train→checkpoint→eval loop has real latency and cost; sequencing it into checkpointed milestones with clear success criteria prevents wasted end-to-end attempts and makes the 45% target reachable within the time box.

anchors.0: No structure; a single monolithic attempt with no intermediate checkpoints or defined success criteria.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only ('train then eval'); no explicit milestone gates or per-step done-conditions.
anchors.5: Clear ordered stages (baseline eval → first training run → eval → iterate) with a stated target per stage.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete pass/fail check (baseline reproduces ~26%; first run beats base; each iteration must exceed prior best), with early cheap milestones de-risking expensive ones and a decision rule for when to stop tuning.
anchors.10: A crisp, budget-aware milestone hierarchy that front-loads the cheapest highest-information checks, defines quantitative gates and expected score deltas per milestone, and sequences experiments so each result informs the next — visibly kept current as the run progresses.

dimensions.name: IFEval harness & score-trust design
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a trustworthy way to measure binary_strict on IFEval (correct renderer, correct scoring, enough samples) and confirming a claimed checkpoint truly hits the number — beyond just trusting a training loss curve.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deliverable is defined entirely by a measured eval score; a renderer mismatch or a mis-wired scorer can make the agent chase a phantom improvement or under-report a real one, and a checkpoint written to the file without a trusted eval may not actually clear 45%.

anchors.0: Never measures IFEval independently; relies on training loss or a single unchecked number, or writes a checkpoint URI it never evaluated.
anchors.3: Runs some eval but with unverified renderer/scoring; treats a noisy one-off number as ground truth with no baseline sanity-check.
anchors.5: Has a working IFEval eval that reproduces the ~26% baseline, and re-evaluates candidate checkpoints on it before claiming an improvement.
anchors.8: Eval harness is validated against the known baseline, uses the eval renderer consistent with training, accounts for sampling noise (adequate sample size / determinism), and gates every 'new best' on a real re-measured score — plus guards against overfitting the metric given the no-contamination rule.
anchors.10: Rigorous, self-auditing verification: baseline reproduced and cross-checked, sampling variance quantified so improvements are distinguished from noise, held-out/generalization checks used to ensure gains aren't renderer or data artifacts, and every checkpoint written to best_checkpoint.txt is backed by a reproducible, trusted measurement of the exact reported metric.

dimensions.name: Budget-aware progress & best-so-far tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of best-score-so-far vs the 45% target and remaining time (via timer.sh), and detecting when runs are plateauing, regressing, or thrashing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Compute/time is bounded and remote; without tracking best-so-far against target and time left, the agent can over-invest in a dead-end approach or run out of budget with an un-persisted or sub-target result.

anchors.0: No tracking of scores across runs or time remaining; never consults the timer; loses track of which checkpoint is best.
anchors.3: Occasionally notes a score but no running comparison to target or budget; timer ignored until too late.
anchors.5: Keeps a clear record of each run's score vs the 45% target and checks remaining time periodically to inform effort.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of experiments (config → score), always knows the current best and gap-to-target, checks timer.sh at decision points, and flags plateaus/regressions instead of repeating them.
anchors.10: Continuous, calibrated situational awareness: quantifies marginal score gain per unit budget, projects whether the current trajectory reaches 45% in the time left, recognizes diminishing returns or circular tuning early, and reallocates effort accordingly — never surprised by the clock.

dimensions.name: Approach revision on evidence
dimensions.description: Revising data mix, method (SFT vs RL), hyperparameters, or renderer when eval evidence shows the current approach isn't moving toward 45%, rather than repeating a falsified recipe.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First-choice data or hyperparameters rarely clear a +19-point gain on the first try; the agent must diagnose why a run underperformed and change the right lever, not grind the same config.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same run/config regardless of results; ignores disconfirming eval scores.
anchors.3: Makes random or superstitious changes after a poor result without diagnosing cause; changes many things at once so nothing is learned.
anchors.5: Responds to a weak eval by adjusting a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) and re-testing, with a basic rationale.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the likely cause of underperformance (e.g., renderer mismatch, wrong data, under/over-training) and makes targeted, one-variable-informed changes, abandoning approaches shown not to transfer.
anchors.10: Treats each run as an experiment: forms hypotheses, changes levers deliberately to isolate effects, updates its mental model of what drives IFEval gains, and pivots decisively (including switching method) when evidence falsifies the current path — while preserving prior best results.

dimensions.name: Best-checkpoint persistence discipline
dimensions.description: Keeping /app/best_checkpoint.txt continuously updated with a valid Tinker sampler-checkpoint URI for the true best-so-far, so a timeout or crash never zeroes an achieved score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires immediately persisting each new best in the exact URI format; a great model that is never written (or written in the wrong format, or not updated when surpassed) yields no credit under the hard deadline.

anchors.0: Never writes best_checkpoint.txt, or writes a malformed/non-sampler URI.
anchors.3: Writes the file once late in the run; not kept in sync with the actual best; format not verified.
anchors.5: Writes a correctly-formatted sampler-checkpoint URI for a genuinely good checkpoint and updates it when clearly beaten.
anchors.8: Updates the file promptly on each verified new best in the exact required format, treating persistence as a first-class step so the deliverable is always valid mid-run.
anchors.10: Disciplined, defensive persistence: every verified best is written immediately in the correct URI form, the write is confirmed, stale/worse URIs are never left in place, and the file always reflects the true best even across interruptions near the deadline.
